title: Fostering success in the classroom
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino revisits how teachers make students feel successful, prompted by Peps McCrea's point in Motivated Teaching that motivation depends on students attributing success to their own effort, not to easy tasks or heavy support. She audits her own habits and finds four that quietly undermine genuine success: endless over-simple Do Now questions, only giving reluctant learners easy tasks, hinting at test questions during revision, and starting homework in lesson time. For each she describes what she does now, such as activating prior knowledge in the Do Now, checking readiness by cold call and mini-whiteboards before challenging independent work, and building assessments on core content so no 'cheating' is needed. The move is a candid self-critique rather than a prescription. Her conclusion is that teachers should support students toward effortful success, not carry them to the end goal.
points: Success only motivates when students can attribute it to their own effort, so tasks made too easy or too supported produce a hollow feeling of achievement.
Over-simple recall questions repeated across lessons bore students; a Do Now that activates relevant prior knowledge shows why facts matter and adds productive effort.
Low expectations for low prior-attaining classes were partly a behaviour-management problem, and clear consistent routines made higher challenge possible.
Previewing test questions in revision feels kind but teaches students they can only succeed with the teacher's help; well-written assessments tied to core content remove the temptation.
Doing homework in class removes the independence homework is meant to build and makes it hard to judge whether students really tried.
quotes: I started to recognise that there were a lot of things I did that were preventing my students from experiencing true success- success they could genuinely attribute to their own effort.
Students ended up bored because although they could answer the simple questions, they couldn’t see why they were important or if they linked to anything further.
I am ashamed to think that I once had the lowest expectations of my low prior-attaining students.
But once again, this form of success is not attributable to their own effort. Even if they do succeed, students now feel as though they can only do so with our help.
Basing teaching and assessments on core questions and key content ensures that students are well prepared without the teacher feeling the need to ‘cheat’ so their students can succeed.

Homework is a way for students to work independently, away from the teacher’s support. This trains them to develop good habits, which will help massively when they revise independently for their exams, but also beyond school.
Our job is support them to get there, not to carry them to the end goal.
